## United States Court of Appeals, Eleventh Circuit.
John Henry Thompson, Christopher Michael Carr, Riley B. Liu, Elijah J. O'Kelley, Logan B. Winkles, Georgia Department of Law, Attorney General's Office, Atlanta, GA, for Defendant-Appellant.
### No. 25-12436

### Decided: October 15, 2026

### Before Newsom, Luck, and Tjoflat, Circuit Judges.
## United States Court of Appeals, Eleventh Circuit.
NetChoice, an Internet trade organization, sued the state, alleging that SB 351 violates the First Amendment both on its face and as applied to its members, is unconstitutionally vague, and is preempted by § 230 of the Communications Decency Act. Finding that it lacked sufficient facts to evaluate an as-applied challenge, the district court decided NetChoice's facial First Amendment, vagueness, and preemption challenges.
The court concluded that SB 351 likely violated the First Amendment on its face, was unconstitutionally vague, and was preempted by § 230, and accordingly enjoined the state from enforcing it.

In particular, it concluded that SB 351 was likely (1) a content-based speech restriction that failed strict scrutiny, (2) unconstitutionally vague, and (3) preempted by § 230. Finding that NetChoice had also met the remaining requirements for obtaining a preliminary injunction, the court enjoined the state from enforcing the challenged provisions of SB 351.

 A federal appeals court has restored Georgia’s ban on giving food and drinks to people waiting in line to vote, sending the legal fight back to a lower court for another look. 

  The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta ruled Monday, Dec. 1, to cancel a preliminary injunction that had blocked enforcement of the law for the past two years. That injunction was issued by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia.

  In its decision, the three-judge panel said a recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling—Moody v. NetChoice, LLC—changed how lower courts must evaluate broad, “facial” challenges to state laws. The appeals court said the district court did not apply that analysis, and directed the case back to the district court for further review.

  The ban was passed by Georgia’s GOP-controlled General Assembly in 2021 as part of the state’s elections overhaul known as Senate Bill 202. One provision drew national attention: a restriction on giving voters “any money or gifts, including, but not limited to, food and drink,” while they are in line at polling places.

  Supporters of the law argue the restriction helps prevent improper influence around polling locations. In response to Monday’s ruling, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger praised the decision, saying it reinforces the state’s authority to protect voters from interference at the polls.

  Civil rights groups have challenged the ban, calling it a barrier to voting. Separately, the U.S. Department of Justice had also sued over the law, arguing it violated the Voting Rights Act—though that lawsuit was later dropped.

Plaintiffs, NetChoice and the Computer & Communications Industry Association (together, “NetChoice”)—are trade associations that represent internet and social-media companies. They sued the Florida officials charged with enforcing S.B. 7072 under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. They sought to enjoin enforcement of Sections 106.072 and 501.2041 on a number of grounds, including, that the law’s provisions (1) violate the social-media companies’ right to free speech under the First Amendment and (2) are preempted by federal law.   The Eleventh Circuit held that the district court did not abuse its discretion when it preliminarily enjoined those provisions of S.B. 7072 that are substantially likely to violate the First Amendment. But the district court did abuse its discretion when it enjoined provisions of S.B. 7072 that aren’t likely unconstitutional.   The court reasoned that it is substantially likely that social-media companies—even the biggest ones—are “private actors” whose rights the First Amendment protects, that their so-called “content-moderation” decisions constitute protected exercises of editorial judgment and that the provisions of the new Florida law that restrict large platforms’ ability to engage in content moderation unconstitutionally burden that prerogative. The court further concluded that it is substantially likely that one of the law’s particularly onerous disclosure provisions—which would require covered platforms to provide a “thorough rationale” for each and every content-moderation decision they make—violates the First Amendment. However, because it is unlikely that the law’s remaining disclosure provisions violate the First Amendment, the companies are not entitled to preliminary injunctive relief with respect to them. # NetChoice Vows to Keep Fighting for Georgians’ Online Rights After Eleventh Circuit Lifts SB 351 Injunction
...
ATLANTA—The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit today vacated the preliminary injunction blocking Georgia’s SB 351 in NetChoice v. Carr, our challenge to the state’s law restricting user access to lawful speech online.

“While we are disappointed in the Eleventh Circuit’s ruling, the court notably did not hold that SB 351 is constitutional,” said Paul Taske, Director of the NetChoice Litigation Center.

“As we evaluate our next legal steps, we remain committed to fighting for Georgians’ right to free expression online and ensuring parents, not the government, stay in charge of decisions for their families.”

This means that when the law goes into effect, social media websites will have to verify the ages of all their Georgia users, forcing Georgians of every age to hand over sensitive personal information just to access lawful speech online. Beyond the constitutional concerns of requiring users to submit government-issued identification to exercise First Amendment rights, age-verification mandates could put Georgians’ personal information at risk. SB 351 also bars Georgians under 16 from creating accounts without parental consent and restricts how services can serve ads to younger users.

Rather than promoting unconstitutional legislation, NetChoice urges Georgia to invest in law enforcement to stop predators, implement digital safety education in schools, and create parent education campaigns about the resources already available to help parents guide their children’s online experiences, all solutions that are a part of NetChoice’s Digital Safety Shield for America.

# Georgia's Social Media Age-Gating Law Is Back in Play: What the Eleventh Circuit Ruled, and What Comes Next

On October 15, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction that had blocked Georgia's social media age-verification law for more than a year. The ruling in NetChoice v. Attorney General, State of Georgia clears the way for the state to enforce SB 351.

What SB 351 requires

Georgia enacted SB 351 in 2024. It requires covered social media platforms to (1) make "commercially reasonable efforts" to verify the age of every account holder; (2) bar children under 16 from holding accounts without a parent's consent; and (3) stop targeting under-16 users with ads based on anything other than age and location. The statute exempts many services (email, streaming, online shopping, gaming, and more), so coverage turns on a platform's "predominant or exclusive function."

NetChoice, a trade group whose members include Meta, X, Reddit, and YouTube, sued in May 2025. Judge Amy Totenberg of the Northern District of Georgia enjoined the law before its July 1, 2025 effective date. She found it likely unconstitutional, void for vagueness, and preempted by Section 230.

What the Eleventh Circuit decided

A panel of Judges Newsom, Luck, and Tjoflat agreed that NetChoice has standing to sue for its members, then reversed on every merits point.

The opinion turns on Moody v. NetChoice, the Supreme Court's 2024 decision requiring a facial First Amendment challenger to map the full range of a law's applications and show that the unconstitutional ones "substantially outweigh" the constitutional ones. The panel sorted covered platforms into three groups: "conventional" platforms hosting fully protected speech, "hybrid" platforms like X and Reddit that also host pornography (which is unprotected as to minors), and hypothetical "rogue" platforms hosting only unprotected speech. keenable.snippet:
# Carr Secures Major Victory in Defense of Georgia’s Social Media Law
ATLANTA, GA — Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr has secured a major victory in defense of SB 351, Georgia’s law that requires parental consent before social media platforms can enter into account agreements with kids aged 15 and younger. The law was previously challenged by NetChoice, the social media industry’s trade association, and the district court issued a preliminary injunction blocking the law’s enforcement.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit issued its opinion in Carr’s favor on Thursday, Oct. 15 following oral arguments earlier this year. With this ruling, the Eleventh Circuit vacated the prior preliminary injunction sought by NetChoice, paving the way for SB 351 to take full effect.

In 2024, the General Assembly passed a law requiring covered social media platforms to verify users' ages and, if under the age of 16, to secure parental consent before providing the child with an account. NetChoice sued, alleging that SB 351 is unconstitutional and moving to block its enforcement. The district court issued a preliminary injunction on June 26, 2025, and Carr filed a notice of appeal immediately thereafter. On Oct. 15, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction and sent the case back to district court for further proceedings.
The Court held that NetChoice's facial First Amendment challenge failed because the trade association offered no evidence backing up its allegation that SB 351's enforcement against most of the platforms it covers would be unconstitutional. The Court also reversed the district court's holdings that aspects of SB 351 were void for vagueness and preempted by Section 230.

If anything, Act 564 undermines free enterprise by threatening marketplaces where many small businesses find and grow their customer base. We’re confident the Eleventh Circuit will agree and keep the law on pause as our case proceeds.”

ultimate.title: Carr Secures Major Victory in Defense of Georgia’s Social Media Law
ultimate.snippet:
# Carr Secures Major Victory in Defense of Georgia’s Social Media Law
ATLANTA, GA — Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr has secured a major victory in defense of SB 351, Georgia’s law that requires parental consent before social media platforms can enter into account agreements with kids aged 15 and younger. The law was previously challenged by NetChoice, the social media industry’s trade association, and the district court issued a preliminary injunction blocking the law’s enforcement.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit issued its opinion in Carr’s favor on Thursday, Oct. 15 following oral arguments earlier this year. With this ruling, the Eleventh Circuit vacated the prior preliminary injunction sought by NetChoice, paving the way for SB 351 to take full effect.

In 2024, the General Assembly passed a law requiring covered social media platforms to verify users' ages and, if under the age of 16, to secure parental consent before providing the child with an account. NetChoice sued, alleging that SB 351 is unconstitutional and moving to block its enforcement. The district court issued a preliminary injunction on June 26, 2025, and Carr filed a notice of appeal immediately thereafter. On Oct. 15, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction and sent the case back to district court for further proceedings.
The Court held that NetChoice's facial First Amendment challenge failed because the trade association offered no evidence backing up its allegation that SB 351's enforcement against most of the platforms it covers would be unconstitutional. The Court also reversed the district court's holdings that aspects of SB 351 were void for vagueness and preempted by Section 230.
